text: John Graham Lough (8 January 1798 – 8 April 1876) was an English sculptor renowned for his funerary monuments and portrait sculptures, as well as ideal classical male and female figures. Born at Black Hedley Port, Greenhead near Consett, County Durham, he was one of eleven children, the son of William Lough of Aycliff, County Durham, and Barbara Clementson of Dalton, Northumberland. His father was a farmer near Hexham, and Lough may have worked as a farmer in his youth. He later apprenticed to a stonemason at Shotley Field near Newcastle upon Tyne and worked in Newcastle as an ornamental sculptor, carving decorations for the building of the city's Literary and Philosophical Society. In 1825, he traveled to London by sea to study the Elgin Marbles at the British Museum, taking lodgings in Burleigh Street, above a greengrocer's shop, where he began moulding his colossal statue of Milo of Croton, inspired by the Elgin Marbles and Michelangelo’s work. In 1826, with support from John Thomas Smith, he joined the Royal Society Schools and became the protégé of painter Benjamin Haydon, exhibiting the completed statue the following year. This work so impressed London society that it brought him numerous patrons and established his career; a later 1863 bronze version of the statue survives at Blagdon, Northumberland. From 1826, he began exhibiting ideal figures and heads at the Royal Academy. Between 1834 and 1838, he spent time in Rome, where his portrait style was influenced by Neo-classicism. He received a provisional commission to carve four granite lions for the base of Nelson's Column, but in 1846, after consulting with the column’s designer William Railton, he withdrew due to unwillingness to work under the architect’s constraints; the commission was later given to Edwin Landseer, with assistance from Carlo Marochetti, who completed it in 1867. He was a close friend of surgeon Campbell De Morgan, who sat with Lough as he lay dying of pneumonia; a bust of De Morgan by Lough is held by the Middlesex Hospital medical school and on display there. Lough is buried in Kensal Green Cemetery, London. One of his younger brothers, Thomas, was a talented musician, artist, and poet, best known for "The Ramshaw Flood" (1848), but fell into vagrancy and poverty, dying at Lanchester Workhouse just one year after John Graham Lough’s death. His public works include a statue of Lord Collingwood in Tynemouth, a memorial to Thomas Noon Talfourd in the Shire Hall, Stafford, and a bronze George Stephenson memorial of 1862 opposite the North of England Institute of Mining and Mechanical Engineers in Newcastle upon Tyne. In London, he produced monuments to Henry Montgomery Lawrence and Bishop Middleton in St Paul's Cathedral, and created the Queen Victoria and Prince Albert for the Royal Exchange. In Canterbury Cathedral, he was responsible for the monuments to Bishop Broughton and Lt Col Frederick Mackeson. He produced many ideal works on classical, historical, and literary themes, including a series of marble statues of Shakespearean subjects for his chief patron, Matthew, 4th Baronet Ridley. Despite his prolific output, Lough was controversial, as his work divided opinion; the Literary Gazette hailed his first exhibition as a demonstration of "extraordinary genius" and later praised a sculptural group as one that "nineteen out of twenty people would prefer ... to any other work in the exhibition," while the Art Journal was fiercely critical, describing his statue of Queen Victoria for the Royal Exchange as "an odiously coarse production, in which not one feature of the Queen is recognisable" and of such "gross vulgarity" that it exceeded "the worst production that has ever been publicly exhibited."
